Molecule

 Home Chemistry
OurBigBook.com Words: 12k Articles: 163
A molecule, using the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) convention, is an electrically neutral entity containing two or more chemical atoms. Its constituents form a bound unit through chemical bonds; merely drawing a boundary around neighboring particles does not make a molecule. The neutrality requirement concerns total electric charge, not the absence of internal charge separation: water is a polar molecule with zero total electric charge.[ref]
One water molecule, H2​O, contains two hydrogen and one oxygen chemical atom. One molecular oxygen molecule, O2​, contains two oxygen chemical atoms; a molecule need not contain different chemical elements. One carbon dioxide molecule, CO2​, contains one carbon and two oxygen chemical atoms. The molecular formula records these inventories, while molecular geometry describes their arrangement. Water and carbon dioxide are chemical compounds; molecular oxygen is a form of one chemical element.
Ordinary crystalline sodium chloride, NaCl, contains an extended arrangement of sodium cations Na+ and chlorine anions Cl−. Its formula unit specifies one of each for compositional accounting, without selecting a unique isolated pair. Bulk neutrality therefore does not imply a material consists of neutral molecules. This statement concerns the ionic crystal; the physical state and conditions matter when deciding what particles a chemical formula represents.[ref]
A polyatomic ion is a charged bound group of chemical atoms, such as hydronium, H3​O+. A molecular ion formed by removing an electron from intact water, H2​O∙+, retains the same atom inventory but has net electric charge +e. Neither satisfies the neutral-molecule definition. Distinguishing these entities makes molecular count and amount of substance and mass spectrometry interpretable: say whether the count is of chemical atoms, neutral molecules, ions, or formula units.
The useful surprise is that a molecule can be treated as one particle for motion and counting while retaining internal structure. Its molar mass connects a particle inventory to bulk mass; molecular rotation and molecular vibration reveal internal organization. The continuum approximation uses bulk fields in place of individual molecular positions and motions.

Molecule bookkeeping

Words: 155
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Four water molecules contain eight hydrogen and four oxygen chemical atoms, twelve constituent chemical atoms altogether. Counting the constituents does not mean they have been separated by breaking chemical bonds. The same sample has different counts because the specified entities differ.
For N water molecules, their amount of substance is n=N/NA​, while the constituent hydrogen and oxygen inventories correspond to 2n and n respectively. The exact Avogadro constant is NA​=6.02214076×1023mol−1. The mole applies to specified entities, including chemical atoms, molecules, and ions.[ref] Thus four water molecules correspond to approximately 6.6422×10−24mol of water, but twice that amount of substance of constituent hydrogen chemical atoms. A macroscopic conversion through measured mass additionally needs the relevant molar mass, as in water mass to molecular count.

Single-molecule experiment

Words: 523 Articles: 4
Molecule OurBigBook.com
A single-molecule experiment resolves a response attributable to an individual molecule, rather than only an average over many molecules. Optical detection need not resolve its constituent chemical atoms in an image: repeated photon absorption by the same molecule can produce a measurable response. One detected photon is not automatically one different molecule.
The measured channel matters. Direct photon absorption detection measures a change in transmitted light. Fluorescence detection collects photons emitted after excitation; a fluorescence excitation spectrum varies the illuminating frequency while observing that emission. Both can probe excitation, but their backgrounds and readouts differ. A labeled particle cartoon explains the interpretation; it supplies no experimental evidence by itself.
Such measurements expose differences that a population average can conceal. Suppose two groups of molecules switch between different internal quantum states. Their average response could vary smoothly even though each molecule changes in discrete steps. Resolving an individual response tests that interpretation directly, subject to the measurement's time resolution, sensitivity, and particle assignment. The following experiment makes that assignment through spectral selection and controlled perturbations.

Single-molecule force spectroscopy

Words: 147 Articles: 2
Single-molecule experiment OurBigBook.com
Measure the force and extension of an individual molecular tether under controlled displacement or load. A calibrated cantilever or optical trap converts deflection to force. Synthetic polymer stretching provides a nonbiological application; the observed curve also contains instrument and attachment compliance, and its loading-rate dependence can distinguish equilibrium elasticity from activated events.

Force clamp

Words: 60
Single-molecule force spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A measurement protocol that holds applied force approximately constant while allowing displacement to vary. Feedback can adjust an actuator in response to a calibrated load signal; alternatively, a passive field gradient can be sufficiently uniform over the displacement range. Finite feedback bandwidth, drift and spatial force variation limit the approximation. This differs from fixing actuator position or prescribing a force ramp.

Cantilever compliance correction (F=kc​d,x=Z−d)

Words: 40
Single-molecule force spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
For a simple single-tether geometry, imposed displacement Z divides into cantilever deflection d and molecular extension x. Applying the displayed correction prevents attributing the instrument's stretch to the molecule. Geometric offsets, handles and substrate compliance require additional calibrated terms.

Single-molecule absorption in a molecular crystal

Words: 221
Single-molecule experiment OurBigBook.com
In 1989, William E. Moerner and Lothar Kador reported individual pentacene absorbers in para-terphenyl in Optical detection and spectroscopy of single molecules in a solid by W. E. Moerner and L. Kador (pp. 2535–2538). Different local environments spread photon absorption frequencies; tuning into the sparse wings selected few resonant molecules despite many molecules in the illuminated volume.
Their tunable dye laser focused through a 0.85 numerical aperture lens onto a 100–200μm crystal immersed in superfluid helium at 1.6K. Frequency modulation accompanied either a 5kHz electric field between coated sapphire disks, detected at 10kHz, or a 2MHz quartz shear transducer. An avalanche photodiode measured transmitted-light photon absorption, not fluorescence. Double modulation suppressed residual laser amplitude background.[ref]
Repeated scans gave the predicted modulated line shape. Blank crystals and off-resonance scans gave background; changing modulation frequency expanded and contracted the feature as predicted. Agreement between both perturbation methods supported the individual-absorber inference. The authors acknowledged out-of-focus molecules and the unlikely alternative of multiple absorbers with exactly coincident frequencies.[ref]
This is evidence for a selected absorber in a prepared, known chemical substance and host. It does not establish arbitrary unknown molecule identity from one spectral feature, provide an atom-resolved photograph, or count every molecule in the crystal. A measurement sensitive to only a narrow excitation range cannot detect a molecule whose transition lies outside that range. This distinction separates the total particle inventory from the number responding to a particular probe.

Molecular rotation

Words: 3k Articles: 25
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Molecular rotation changes a molecule's orientation. Its rotational kinetic energy depends on the arrangement and masses of its chemical atoms. A rigid rotor freezes internal distances to isolate this motion; rotational spectroscopy tests the resulting energy eigenvalues through transitions between quantum states. The molecular beam electric resonance experiment provides a complementary probe of the coupling to an electric field.

Vibration-rotation interaction (Bv​=Be​−αe​(v+1/2))

Words: 77 Articles: 1
Molecular rotation OurBigBook.com
The dependence of rotational energy on the vibrational state. For a diatomic molecule a common leading approximation is Bv​=Be​−αe​(v+1/2), so vibrational satellites can have different rotational line spacings.

Polyatomic vibration-rotation interaction (Bv​=Be​−∑i​αi​(vi​+di​/2))

Words: 48
Vibration-rotation interaction OurBigBook.com
The first-order dependence of a polyatomic rotational constant on vibrational occupations vi​, where di​ is the degeneracy of normal mode i. The factor di​/2 accounts for all of that mode's zero-point energy. A single band's change in rotational constant generally determines one αi​, rather than every zero-point correction needed for Be​.

Rigid rotor

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Molecular rotation OurBigBook.com
A rigid rotor models rotational motion with fixed internal separations. Its use in the synthetic Stark effect figure omits vibrational motion and additional interactions in real molecules.
Rigidity fixes the molecular geometry, not the orientation, and does not require a spherical mass distribution. Remove motion of the centre of mass, choose principal axes of the inertia tensor, and write the classical rotational kinetic energy as
Trot​=21​(Ia​ωa2​+Ib​ωb2​+Ic​ωc2​)=2Ia​La2​​+2Ib​Lb2​​+2Ic​Lc2​​.
(1)
Here Ia​,Ib​,Ic​ are the principal moments of inertia, ωa​,ωb​,ωc​ components of angular velocity, and La​,Lb​,Lc​ components of angular momentum. Quantization replaces these last components by angular momentum operators. Different principal moments of inertia produce different spectra: the single-constant linear rigid rotor is a special case, not a formula for every molecule.[ref]

Rotational line spacing and diatomic bond length (r=h/(4π2μΔν)​)

Words: 51
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For a rigid heteronuclear diatomic rotor, EJ​=ℏ2J(J+1)/(2I) and electric-dipole absorption has ΔJ=+1. Therefore the J′→J′−1 line frequency is hJ′/(4π2I) and adjacent absorption lines are spaced by h/(4π2I). With reduced mass μ, the bond-length estimate is r=I/μ​. The conversion assumes frequency rather than angular frequency; centrifugal distortion makes real high-J spacings imperfectly uniform.

Planar rigid rotor (Em​=ℏ2m2/(2I))

Words: 73
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
A rigid rotor restricted to one angular coordinate ϕ. Single-valued spatial states eimϕ have m∈Z and energy Em​=ℏ2m2/(2I), with moment of inertia I. The zero-angular-momentum level has state degeneracy one; every nonzero ∣m∣ has two directions. For labelled molecular ends its high-temperature rotational partition function is πT/θrot​​, where θrot​=ℏ2/(2IkB​). Equivalent orientations and nuclear spin statistics require a further molecular counting convention. One quadratic angular momentum gives rotational heat capacity kB​/2 per molecule, rather than kB​ for an unrestricted linear rigid rotor.

Rotational energy (EJ​=ℏ2J(J+1)/(2I))

Words: 50 Articles: 1
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For a linear rigid rotor with moment of inertia I, the energy eigenvalue at angular momentum quantum number J is ℏ2J(J+1)/(2I). Each level has statistical weight 2J+1 before additional symmetry or nuclear-spin restrictions.
Rotational angular momentum (N)
Words: 29
Rotational energy OurBigBook.com
The angular momentum associated with end-over-end molecular rotation. In an open-shell diatomic molecule it is useful to distinguish N from the total J=N+S, which also contains the electronic spin angular momentum.

Rotational symmetry number (σ)

Words: 57
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
The rotational symmetry number corrects a rotational phase-space count for indistinguishable molecular orientations. A linear molecule with identical ends, such as carbon dioxide with identical oxygen isotopes, has σ=2; making its ends isotopically distinct gives σ=1. In the high-temperature linear rigid rotor approximation, qrot​=8π2IkT/(σh2). Holding the spectrum otherwise fixed, doubling σ lowers molar rotational entropy by Rlog2.

Linear rigid rotor (EJ​=ℏ2J(J+1)/(2I))

Words: 754 Articles: 4
Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For a diatomic molecule, let m1​,m2​ be the two masses and r their fixed separation. The distances from the centre of mass are r1​=m2​r/(m1​+m2​) and r2​=m1​r/(m1​+m2​). A perpendicular axis through the centre of mass therefore has moment of inertia
I=m1​r12​+m2​r22​=μr2,μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​.
(2)
The reduced mass μ here is not the electric dipole moment, for which we use d. For a longer linear molecule, replace μr2 by ∑i​mi​ρi2​, where ρi​ is each distance along the axis from the centre of mass. In the point-mass idealization, the axial moment of inertia is zero; turning about that axis changes no nuclear positions, so no independent axial rotational degree of freedom is included.
For the field-free linear rigid rotor, assume a fixed internal quantum state with no electronic angular momentum or electronic spin, and omit couplings to nuclear spin. The rotational Hamiltonian is Hrot​=L2/(2I). Its orientation wavefunctions are spherical harmonics YJM​, and its angular momentum eigenstates satisfy
L2YJM​=ℏ2J(J+1)YJM​,Lz​YJM​=ℏMYJM​,EJ​=2Iℏ2​J(J+1)=hBJ(J+1),
(3)
where J=0,1,2,… and M=−J,−J+1,…,J. Each EJ​ belongs to 2J+1 angular momentum eigenstates distinguished by the magnetic quantum number M, an instance of degenerate energy levels. The Planck constant is h=2πℏ; B is the frequency-valued rotational constant. Notice that the energy eigenvalues scale as J(J+1), not J2.
Subtracting consecutive energy eigenvalues gives
νJ→J+1​=hEJ+1​−EJ​​=2B(J+1).
(4)
Thus increasing level gaps produce a regularly spaced series of lines at 2B,4B,6B,…, with spacing 2B. Allowed positions do not guarantee that every line is visible: electric-dipole selection rules, occupation of the initial quantum state, and instrument response also matter.
Rotational temperature (θr​=ℏ2/(2IkB​))
Words: 52
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For a linear rigid rotor, rotational temperature expresses the rotational energy constant in kelvins: EJ​=kB​θr​J(J+1), where I is the perpendicular moment of inertia. With all integer J≥0 allowed and degeneracies 2J+1, its rotational canonical partition function is Z=∑J​(2J+1)e−θr​J(J+1)/T. It approaches 1+3e−2θr​/T at low temperature and T/θr​ at high temperature. The latter limit gives mean rotational energy kB​T and heat capacity kB​ per rotor.
Rotational constant (B=h/(8π2I))
Words: 102
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
In this article the rotational constant is a frequency,
B=8π2Ih​.
(5)
Its dimensions are s−1, since the Planck constant has dimensions kgm2s−1 and a moment of inertia has dimensions kgm2. Some authors instead call hB=ℏ2/(2I) the energy-valued rotational constant; this is the convention in the earlier synthetic molecular beam electric resonance diagram. A third convention uses the spectroscopic wavenumber B=B/c, with c the speed of light. Always check units before using ν=2B(J+1).
If B is known and the two masses are specified, the rigid two-atom model gives the bond length r=h/(8π2μB)​. This is why rotational spectroscopy can constrain molecular geometry. A real fitted constant can depend on molecular vibration, so this inference alone does not establish an equilibrium bond length.
Pure rotational electric-dipole selection rules (ΔJ=±1)
Words: 126
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
For the field-free, spin-free linear rigid rotor in one fixed internal quantum state, the electric-dipole interaction is −d⋅E(t). A nonzero permanent electric dipole moment along the molecular axis allows pure rotational photon absorption with ΔJ=+1 and photon emission with ΔJ=−1. The matrix element between initial and final quantum states must be nonzero: the existence of an energy gap alone is insufficient. Relative to a chosen z axis, polarization of an electromagnetic wave along z selects ΔM=0; transverse polarization of an electromagnetic wave permits ΔM=±1.[ref]
Hydrogen chloride and carbon monoxide are examples with a permanent electric dipole moment. By symmetry, molecular hydrogen and carbon dioxide have no permanent electric dipole moment in the ideal symmetric internal state. They still rotate and have rotational energy eigenvalues, but the simple permanent-electric dipole spectrum described here is absent. This restriction concerns this interaction and these assumptions, not every possible way of detecting molecular rotation.
Isotope shift of a linear rotor
Words: 213
Linear rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
Changing an isotope changes a mass and therefore the moment of inertia. If the bond length is held fixed, B∝1/μ and every corresponding transition shifts by the same fractional amount. This leading inverse-reduced mass scaling is also used in the more complete diatomic formulation.[ref]
For a deliberately stipulated carbon monoxide example, take m12​=12u, m13​=13u, m16​=16u, u=1.66053906660×10−27kg, r=1.13×10−10m for both isotopic forms, and h=6.62607015×10−34Js. The integer masses are simplifying inputs, not accurate isotopic atomic masses; the shared bond length is an imposed model assumption. Calculation gives

Centrifugal distortion (EJ​/h=BJ(J+1)−D[J(J+1)]2+⋯)

Rigid rotor OurBigBook.com
Real chemical bonds can stretch as molecular rotation increases. The resulting larger moment of inertia lowers the energy eigenvalues relative to a rigid rotor. Within one vibrational quantum state, a leading effective correction is
hEJ​​=Bv​J(J+1)−Dv​[J(J+1)]2+⋯,νJ→J+1​=2Bv​(J+1)−4Dv​(J+1)3+⋯.
(8)
Both Bv​ and Dv​ are in frequency units here; v labels the vibrational quantum state. For positive Dv​, the adjacent-line spacing becomes
νJ+1→J+2​−νJ→J+1​=2Bv​−4Dv​(3J2+9J+7),
(9)
so the departures grow with J. Molecular vibration also changes the effective rotational constant: even the lowest vibrational quantum state does not have motionless atomic nuclei.[ref]
The quartic correction is a limited expansion, not a model to extrapolate to arbitrary J. It is small relative to the rigid contribution only while (Dv​/Bv​)J(J+1)≪1; eventually higher terms, changed internal motion, or chemical bond breaking matter. In the synthetic plot, the largest upper-state label is J=5, giving a stipulated correction ratio of 0.03. No universal maximum valid J follows without a particular molecule and precision target.
The quantum numbers also have limits of meaning. Here J describes spin-free rotation. In a molecule with electronic spin, rotation alone is commonly labelled N, while J includes electronic angular momentum; including nuclear spin introduces additional total-angular momentum labels and resolved splittings. An applied electric field can mix different field-free J states through the Stark effect. For identical atomic nuclei, the Pauli exclusion principle can restrict combinations of rotational and nuclear-spin states. The simple 2J+1 degeneracy and every-integer-J ladder therefore describe the stated idealization, not all observed sublevels.[ref]

Rotational spectroscopy

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Molecular rotation OurBigBook.com
Rotational spectroscopy measures transitions between molecular rotation quantum states, usually in low-pressure gaseous molecules. The measured spectral lines become a molecular fingerprint only after rotational spectral line assignment: identify which transitions belong together, determine their quantum numbers, fit a rotational Hamiltonian, and test additional predictions. Line positions constrain moments of inertia, while rotational state populations and transition coupling determine which lines can be detected.
The simplest ordinary microwave absorption ladder belongs to a polar linear molecule obeying pure rotational electric-dipole selection rules. A homonuclear diatomic molecule has no permanent electric dipole moment in its symmetric internal state, but rotational Raman spectroscopy can probe its rotation through anisotropic electric polarizability. The coupling mechanism must therefore be specified before interpreting a missing spectrum.
The existing linear rigid rotor, rotational constant, isotope shift of a linear rotor, and centrifugal distortion explain the forward model. Molecular structure from rotational constants asks the reverse question: which arrangements of chemical atoms could produce the fitted constants? The NIST trace-gas FTMW validation experiment makes the measurement chain concrete and separates identifying a species from measuring its concentration.

A set of spectral lines associated with transitions between molecular rotational energy levels. A polar linear rigid rotor has electric-dipole transitions with ΔJ=±1; in the ideal model adjacent absorption frequencies are separated by twice the rotational constant in frequency units.

For a polar rigid symmetric top with its permanent dipole on the symmetry axis, electric-dipole pure rotation has ΔJ=±1, ΔK=0. The A−B term cancels within each transition; centrifugal distortion can lift the rigid-model coincidence of different K components.

Rotational spectral line assignment (νm​=2Bm−4Dm3,m=J+1)

Rotational spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A rotational spectral line assignment associates a measured spectral line with a molecule, an internal quantum state, and an initial and final set of quantum numbers. For the spin-free linear rigid rotor, absorption is labelled J→J+1. A regularly spaced group suggests a candidate rotational constant, but the lowest line inside a scanned band need not be 0→1. Several molecules can contribute to the same spectrum, and an apparent missing member can lie outside the band or below the detection threshold.
First determine line centers and their uncertainties from the instrument's readout, accounting for resolved Doppler shifts or hyperfine structure rather than treating every peak as a separate rotational transition. Then propose integer assignments, fit a rotational Hamiltonian, and predict additional spectral lines. For a weakly distorted linear molecule within one vibrational quantum state, the centrifugal distortion model gives the useful diagnostic
νm​=2Bm−4Dm3,2mνm​​=B−2Dm2,m=J+1.
(10)
Here B,D,νm​ are all frequencies in Hz. Correct assignments make the second expression a straight line against m2, with intercept B and slope −2D. This follows by division of the transition formula; no additional model of molecular geometry is required. A direct weighted least squares fit of νm​ to 2Bm−4Dm3 uses the measured uncertainties. If instead the transformed values are fitted, their uncertainties must also be divided by 2m.[ref]
For an original example, stipulate B=5.000000GHz and D=2.000kHz, and suppose a scan covers 38–72GHz. The model places four consecutive transitions at 39.999488, 49.999000, 59.998272, and 69.997256GHz. Their assignments are m=4,5,6,7, hence J=3,4,5,6. An extra stipulated line at 53.2GHz is unrelated to this series. All these frequencies are calculated example inputs, not measured OCS data.
At m=4 and m=7, the transformed values are 4999.936 and 4999.804MHz. Their straight line has slope (4999.804−4999.936)/(49−16)=−0.004MHz, recovering D=0.002MHz and B=5000MHz. Both intermediate transitions satisfy the same line exactly. Merely relabelling the first visible transition 0→1 fails this diagnostic. The model predicts a withheld 7→8 transition at 79.995904GHz: an additional measurement there would test the assignment rather than merely refit the original four lines.
An assignment earns confidence when several independently observed spectral lines, including lines outside the fitted interval, agree within uncertainty and expected strong accessible lines are present. Inspect the residual of an inverse problem for each line against J: systematic curvature can signal inadequate centrifugal distortion, whereas isolated discrepancies suggest a blend or wrong assignment. Comparing a known sample, a blank, and an isotope shift of a linear rotor supplies different checks. These are general inference controls; the actual reported controls of the NIST trace-gas FTMW validation experiment are described separately. One isolated match or one fitted rotational constant alone cannot certify molecular identity.

The 2J+1 factor counts magnetic quantum numbers; it does not mean that a whole level is one quantum state. For the stipulated B=5GHz, the most populated levels are J=2 at 3K and J=7 at 30K.
Population alone is insufficient to predict intensity. In weak, unsaturated absorption, the integrated absorption coefficient includes the transition frequency, the squared electric dipole moment matrix element, and the difference of lower and upper substate populations because stimulated emission returns energy to the field. A pulsed FTMW spectroscopy signal additionally depends on excitation, quantum coherence, cavity tuning, and receiver response.[ref]
For an isotropic sample with polarization of an electromagnetic wave along z, write dz​=dcosθ. Normalized spherical harmonics give

The common factor includes d2/3 and cancels upon normalization. This formula describes integrated weak absorption in a thermal, spin-free linear rigid rotor, not arbitrary peak heights. The example's strongest integrated lines originate at J=3 and J=13 for 3 and 30K, respectively: they differ from the most populated levels. A missing line can reflect population, coupling, coverage, or sensitivity; it does not prove that the corresponding quantum state is absent.

The rotational state populations of a spin-free polar linear rigid rotor are proportional to (2J+1)e−θrot​J(J+1)/T. Differentiating their logarithm with respect to continuous J gives the displayed maximum when it is nonnegative. The actual maximum must be selected among nonnegative integers by comparing adjacent populations. This population maximum generally differs from a maximum in measured spectral line intensity.

Molecular structure from rotational constants

Rotational spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Recovering molecular geometry from rotational constants is an inverse problem. In the synthetic assignment, B=5×109Hz gives I=h/(8π2B)≃1.6784×10−45kgm2. For a diatomic molecule with known masses, rotational constant explains how to infer an effective bond length. For a longer linear molecule, one I cannot determine every bond length: several different arrangements can have the same moment of inertia.
For a fixed three-atom linear model with positions 0,a,a+b and positive masses m1​,m2​,m3​, subtracting the centre of mass gives
I=m1​+m2​+m3​m1​m2​a2+m2​m3​b2+m1​m3​(a+b)2​.
(14)
This is one equation for two unknown bond lengths. Even fixing the order of the chemical atoms leaves a family of solutions. Additional isotope substitutions change known masses and supply independent equations, provided the effective molecular geometry can be treated as shared. For nonlinear molecules, three principal moments of inertia give frequency-valued constants A=h/(8π2Ia​), B=h/(8π2Ib​), and C=h/(8π2Ic​); a single evenly spaced comb is generally insufficient.
Vibrational averaging, unresolved hyperfine structure, internal motion, and centrifugal distortion limit structural inference. A ground-vibrational fitted rotational constant is not automatically the equilibrium constant. Ordinary field-free rotational spectroscopy also gives identical spectra for opposite enantiomers under the usual parity-symmetric molecular Hamiltonian; assigning composition and conformation does not by itself determine handedness. Molecular identification from a rich fingerprint can therefore succeed even when a unique full molecular geometry cannot be reconstructed.

Rotational Raman spectroscopy (ΔJ=0,±2)

Words: 238
Rotational spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Rotational Raman spectroscopy observes a frequency change of scattered light associated with molecular rotation. The coupling uses the induced electric dipole moment, dind​=αE, where α is the electric polarizability tensor. For a linear molecule, the useful anisotropy is α∥​−α⊥​: the response differs for an electric field parallel or perpendicular to the molecular axis. A permanent electric dipole moment is not required.[ref]
For the spin-free linear rigid rotor in one internal quantum state, the anisotropic tensor depends quadratically on the molecular direction. Its angular part has even parity and degree two in spherical harmonics. The triangle inequality for coupled angular momenta permits ∣ΔJ∣≤2, and even parity removes odd ΔJ, leaving ΔJ=0,±2. The ΔJ=0 contribution is unshifted light; shifted rotational lines have ΔJ=±2. Consequently the rigid-model Stokes shifts, in ordinary frequency units, are
ΔνJ​=hEJ+2​−EJ​​=B(4J+6),J=0,1,2,….
(15)
Successive allowed shifts are separated by 4B, rather than the 2B absorption spacing of pure rotational electric-dipole selection rules. In spectroscopic wavenumber units replace B by B=B/c and Δν by Δν=Δν/c, using the speed of light in cms−1 for cm−1.
A homonuclear diatomic molecule such as molecular hydrogen has no permanent electric dipole moment in its symmetric internal state, so it lacks the ordinary electric-dipole microwave ladder. Its anisotropic electric polarizability can nevertheless give rotational Raman spectroscopy lines. Nuclear-spin symmetry can change the populations of even and odd J levels, so the spin-free population example above must not be reused unchanged for molecular hydrogen. The method of coupling, as well as the energy eigenvalues, determines what the experiment can see.

Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy

Words: 601 Articles: 2
Rotational spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy excites gaseous molecules with a pulse of electromagnetic radiation, then records the emitted time-dependent electric field. A Fourier transform extracts transition frequencies from the decaying signal. In a cavity implementation, two facing mirrors form a resonator; tuned excitation, receiver electronics and digitization replace the molecule-counting readout of molecular beam electric resonance. The pulsed radiation prepares quantum coherence between rotational quantum states; it does not set the whole gas spinning at one classical angular velocity.
For documented laboratory context, Evolution of Microwave Spectroscopy at the National Bureau of Standards (NBS) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) by F. J. Lovas and others (§5, printed pp. 280–282) describes the NIST cavity instrument, phase-locked sources, mirror tuning and detector-mixer modifications. That account explains one instrument family; it does not establish the electronics of every later commercial spectrometer.
NIST trace-gas FTMW validation experiment
Words: 277
Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
The NIST validation report used 1% carbonyl sulfide in argon to illustrate the readout. A pulsed nozzle injected a molecular beam along a two-mirror cavity. Approximately 1μs excitation prepared quantum coherence; a receiver digitized the decaying electric field, then a Fourier transform produced spectral lines. Counterpropagating cavity waves produced a Doppler shift doublet; its midpoint represents one rest-frame transition.[ref]
The portable electronics used a common microwave source and a 30MHz offset derived from a 10MHz reference. Cavity tuning selects the accessible band; it does not independently calibrate the line's frequency. Absolute accuracy also requires a characterized reference and receiver offset.[ref]
Reported controls included nozzle off/on, carrier-gas changes, and a blind nitrogen mixture. Assigned components were correctly identified. Single-component standards supplied preliminary concentration calibration; one standard per quantified component left response validation incomplete. Condensation and departure from thermal equilibrium in the nozzle were acknowledged limitations.[ref]
The lesson is that rotational spectral line assignment and concentration inference answer different questions. Reproducible frequencies support molecular identity; converting signal size into concentration requires calibrated response under the same transfer and excitation conditions. The thermal absorption example above does not model a nozzle's nonequilibrium populations or the cavity's pulsed response.
Rotational monitoring of deuterium exchange

Fourier transform microwave spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
A distinct experiment in An Automated, Highly Selective Reaction Monitoring Instrument Using Molecular Rotational Resonance Spectroscopy by Ann Adele Byars and others (Figure 1 and Figure 3) tracked exchange of hydrogen for deuterium in ethyl acetoacetate mixed with deuterated methanol. A pump circulated chemical solution through a valve; a calibrated loop injected aliquots into a temperature-controlled inlet, held at room temperature for this exchange experiment. Neon carried the vaporized sample to a cavity spectrometer. Separately recorded broadband spectra and fitted rotational Hamiltonians identified transitions for the four isotopic forms before targeted monitoring.[ref]
The readout was each assigned line's signal over reaction time, normalized by the sum of the four signals. Transitions with the same quantum numbers reduced response-factor differences. A solvent wash addressed observed sample carryover. The signals distinguished the unsubstituted, two singly substituted, and doubly substituted forms. Only one gas-phase structural form was detected; the authors explicitly caution that their readout does not recover the structural chemical equilibrium in chemical solution.[ref]
This example uses nonlinear molecules, so neither the single-constant linear rigid rotor nor the synthetic comb above is a fit to its spectrum. Its connection to the model is the sensitivity of moments of inertia to isotope placement. Line position helps assign a species; signal size additionally depends on sample transfer, initial quantum state populations and instrument response. Matching quantum numbers is a useful control, not a proof of identical response factors. These distinctions explain why resolving species and determining their concentrations are separate inference steps.

Spin isomers of hydrogen
Words: 2k Articles: 10
Homonuclear diatomic molecule OurBigBook.com
Spin isomers of hydrogen are two forms of molecular hydrogen, 1H2​, distinguished by the combined nuclear spin of their two protons. They have the same chemical formula and electronic ground state, but different allowed molecular rotation states. Parahydrogen has total nuclear spin zero and even rotational quantum number J; orthohydrogen has total nuclear spin one and odd J. The difference makes heat capacity a probe of fermionic exchange symmetry, and makes cooling history matter for a tank of molecular hydrogen.
Assume the electronic ground state X1Σg+​ and the vibrational ground state of a free molecule. The electronic factor is symmetric under exchanging the two protons, and the vibrational factor depends only on their separation, so it is also symmetric. These assumptions concern the exchange of protons; the electronic wavefunction separately obeys fermionic exchange symmetry under exchange of electrons. Neglect electronic excitation, vibrational excitation, external fields, and small interactions involving nuclear spin when calculating rotational energy eigenvalues.
The two protons are identical particles with spin 1/2. Their complete wavefunction must change sign under their particle exchange operator. Interchanging the two ends reverses the internuclear direction r, and the spherical harmonic rotational factor satisfies
YJM​(−r)=(−1)JYJM​(r).
(16)
The antisymmetric spin-one-half singlet state therefore requires symmetric, even-J rotation; the symmetric spin-one-half triplet state requires antisymmetric, odd-J rotation. This is exchange symmetry of two identical spin-one-half fermions applied inside a diatomic molecule, not an extra rotational force. A linear rigid rotor may omit spin-dependent splittings while still requiring this restriction on its allowed quantum states.

Interconversion of orthohydrogen and parahydrogen, which changes the coupled nuclear-spin and rotational populations. An active conversion mechanism allows the mole fractions to follow equilibrium as temperature changes; slow conversion instead gives a frozen ortho-para mixture. Whether conversion remains active during a thermal measurement must therefore be distinguished from how the initial sample was prepared.

A sample of mass M initially containing an orthohydrogen fraction xo​ therefore releases Q≃xo​Mℏ2/(mp2​r2) on complete conversion to the lowest parahydrogen level. This estimate neglects the electron contribution to molecular mass and changes of the rotational constant with environment. It describes an internal heat load that external insulation cannot remove.

Normal hydrogen (xo​=3/4,xp​=1/4)

Spin isomers of hydrogen OurBigBook.com
Normal hydrogen denotes the 3:1 orthohydrogen-to-parahydrogen mixture, the high-temperature equilibrium limit. Near room temperature the equilibrium ratio is already close to this limit. A kinetically frozen composition can therefore coexist with rotational thermal equilibrium separately within each species.
The distinction was historically decisive. The institutional account Die Entdeckung des para-Wasserstoffs, in its discussion of the rotational heat capacity, explains that assuming an equilibrating composition missed the observed behavior, whereas freezing the high-temperature ratio reproduced it. It also records Karl Friedrich Bonhoeffer and Paul Harteck's 1929 preparation using a catalyst and thermal conductivity detection.[ref]

A catalyst changes the conversion rate and allows heat removal during cooling; it does not change the free-gas equilibrium weights at a specified temperature. The 1935 primary paper The Spin-Isomerization of Hydrogen at Paramagnetic and Diamagnetic Surfaces, pp. 1251–1252, describes evacuated catalyst samples cooled before admitting molecular hydrogen. Gas samples were analyzed in a glass cell in liquid air: a heated platinum wire and Wheatstone bridge converted changes in thermal conductivity into electrical resistance readings, calibrated against normal hydrogen.[ref]
Its comparison of oxide surfaces supplied a control: specimens exhibiting strong paramagnetism converted the gas much faster than the comparison exhibiting diamagnetism despite all adsorbing molecular hydrogen. Contact time, pressure, and temperature were recorded. This supports a role for surface magnetic properties beyond adsorption alone; it does not identify every microscopic surface site or directly measure nuclear-spin orientations.[ref]
The inference chain is preparation, contact with a specified surface, then a calibrated bulk transport readout of composition. It is distinct from a direct calorimetry measurement of heat capacity: transport and heat capacity can both depend on the spin populations, but they are different measured quantities. Changing the catalyst's own surface structure, introducing magnetic impurities, or changing the detector's gas pressure can confound an uncalibrated comparison. The free-rotor partition functions predict equilibrium populations and stored energy, not the conversion rate on a particular surface.

Molecular vibration

Words: 2k Articles: 25
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Molecular vibration changes internal separations and bond angles, unlike the fixed internal molecular geometry of a rigid rotor. Its coupling to molecular rotation makes measured rotational constants depend on the vibrational quantum state.
A diatomic molecule has one internal stretching coordinate: its two atomic nuclei approach and separate about an equilibrium bond length. The diatomic bond stretch turns this motion into a particularly useful model. The local potential energy curvature supplies the restoring force, while the reduced mass accounts for both moving partners. Thus the same chemical bond can vibrate more slowly after an isotope substitution even when its electronic structure is nearly unchanged.
This separation makes infrared spectroscopy informative: transition frequencies constrain chemical bond stiffness, and isotope scaling of diatomic vibration tests the mass dependence. The University of Florida HCl and DCl FTIR experiment illustrates the measurement. Detectability also requires vibrational infrared activity; having vibrational energy eigenvalues alone does not guarantee an infrared absorption line.

Loss of excess vibrational excitation to other molecular degrees of freedom or to the surroundings. It can occur within one electronic state without photon emission, reducing the energy available to subsequent fluorescence.

A mass-weighted displacement coordinate along an eigenvector of the molecular harmonic force-constant matrix after rigid translations and rotations are removed. An orthonormal normal-mode basis gives kinetic energy 21​∑i​Pi2​ and harmonic potential 21​∑i​ωi2​Qi2​. This use of normal coordinate concerns molecular vibrations, rather than normal coordinates of a spacetime metric.

A positive value makes adjacent level spacings decrease. For an exact Morse oscillator, De​/(hc)=ωe​/(4xe​). Using only two low-lying transitions to extrapolate this identity to a real molecule assumes the higher-order anharmonic terms are negligible all the way to dissociation.

Coordinates belonging to inequivalent irreducible representations cannot have an invariant bilinear cross term. Two copies of the same real irreducible representation can: their componentwise dot product is invariant. Diagonalizing the multiplicity-space force-constant matrix produces the normal modes. Symmetry alone therefore does not require two T2​ coordinate sets to have zero coupling before that diagonalization.

Molecular vibration OurBigBook.com
In the independent harmonic approximation, each diatomic molecule has one bond-stretching quantum harmonic oscillator with energies (n+1/2)ℏω. Write x=ℏω/(kB​T). Its canonical partition function is z=e−x/2/(1−e−x), and differentiating its logarithm gives
Uvib​=Nℏω(21​+ex−11​),CV,vib​=NkB​(ex−1)2x2ex​.
(24)
For T≪ℏω/kB​, excitation is exponentially suppressed and the heat capacity tends to zero. At high temperature it tends to NkB​, one kB​/2 contribution from each quadratic kinetic and potential term. The zero-point energy does not contribute to the derivative with temperature. For a dilute gas whose rotations are already active, adding translation and rotation gives molar CV​≃5R/2 before vibration is activated and 7R/2 afterwards, provided dissociation and electronic excitations are negligible.

Diatomic bond stretch (q=r−re​,ω=k/μ​)

Molecular vibration OurBigBook.com
Let r be the instantaneous bond length, re​>0 its equilibrium value, and q=r−re​ the stretching displacement. Assume one fixed electronic quantum state, a smooth potential energy V(r) with a nondegenerate local minimum at re​, and omit molecular rotation initially. The Taylor series has no linear term because V′(re​)=0:
V(re​+q)=V0​+21​kq2+O(q3),V0​=V(re​),k=V′′(re​)>0.
(25)
Keeping only the quadratic term is the harmonic approximation near a potential minimum. The bond force constant k has units Nm−1. It measures local stiffness; it is not the bond-dissociation energy, which concerns the depth and distant shape of the entire well.
The two-particle relative coordinate explains the reduced mass. For stretching along a fixed axis in a stationary centre of mass frame, let u1​,u2​ be the nuclear displacements from equilibrium. Then u2​−u1​=q and m1​u1​+m2​u2​=0, so
u1​=−m1​+m2​m2​​q,u2​=m1​+m2​m1​​q,T=21​m1​u˙12​+21​m2​u˙22​=21​μq˙​2,μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​.
(26)
Here T is the internal kinetic energy, and m1​,m2​>0 are the two nuclear masses. The lighter partner moves farther; the reduced mass is smaller than either individual mass. The restoring force −dV/dq≃−kq gives simple harmonic motion:
μq¨​=−kq,q(t)=Acos(ωt+ϕ),ω=μk​​,ν=2πω​,νharm​=2πcω​.
(27)
The angular frequency is ω, the ordinary frequency is ν, and νharm​ is the corresponding spectroscopic wavenumber; c is the speed of light. Use c in cms−1 to obtain νharm​ in cm−1. The symbol k here is a bond force constant, not an angular wavenumber.
For an original dimensionless example, choose m1​=m2​=2 and k=4 in consistent model units. Then μ=1 and ω=2. Releasing at q(0)=0.1 with q˙​(0)=0 gives q(t)=0.1cos(2t) and u1​=−q/2, u2​=q/2. Each atomic nucleus moves only half the stretching amplitude, while the conserved internal mechanical energy above V0​ is 21​k(0.1)2=0.02. Fixing one partner instead would give ω=2​, demonstrating why a one-body calculation changes the model.

Bond force constant (k=V′′(re​))

Diatomic bond stretch OurBigBook.com
The bond force constant is the curvature of the effective potential energy at the equilibrium bond length. For a diatomic bond stretch, it plays the role of a spring constant. Its definition is local: two wells with the same curvature can have different bond-dissociation energies.

Harmonic vibrational energy levels (Ev​=V0​+ℏω(v+1/2))

Words: 216
Diatomic bond stretch OurBigBook.com
Quantizing the stretching coordinate gives a quantum harmonic oscillator with reduced mass μ:
H=V0​−2μℏ2​dq2d2​+21​kq2,Ev​=V0​+ℏω(v+21​),v=0,1,2,….
(28)
Here v is the vibrational quantum number and ℏ=h/(2π) the reduced Planck constant. Consecutive energy eigenvalues have gap ℏω; the ground state has zero-point energy ℏω/2 above the well minimum. The offset V0​ cancels from every transition energy.
A short proof uses creation and annihilation operators: with ℓ=ℏ/(μω)​, write q=ℓ(a+a†)/2​. The Quantum Hamiltonian becomes H−V0​=ℏω(a†a+1/2). Nonnegativity of a†a gives the lowest level; repeated application of a† raises its energy by ℏω each time. This also gives ⟨q⟩v​=0 and
⟨q2⟩v​=μωℏ​(v+21​).
(29)
The ground state therefore has a nonzero spread of bond lengths, even though its mean stretching displacement vanishes. A stationary energy eigenstate has a time-independent position probability density; the classical oscillation curve is not a trajectory of an atomic nucleus in that state.
The parabolic model formally extends q to the whole real line, whereas an actual bond length satisfies r>0. It is useful for low levels concentrated near re​, with typical stretching displacements much smaller than re​. It fails near breakup of the chemical bond and when neglected anharmonicity becomes substantial.

These are chosen mass number approximations, not measured atomic masses or natural-abundance averages. With the same chlorine isotope in both molecules,
μHCl​=3635​u,μDCl​=3770​u,ωHCl​ωDCl​​=νharm,HCl​νharm,DCl​​=μDCl​μHCl​​​=7237​​≈0.716860.

This is the isotope scaling of diatomic vibration prediction. Doubling the light partner's mass nearly doubles the reduced mass, lowering the frequency by about 28.3%. The factor differs from 1/2​ because the chlorine partner also moves.
For the same small initial stretch A and zero velocity, both models start with the same internal mechanical energy kA2/2, but the DCl oscillation period is longer by 72/37​≈1.394972. In the centre of mass frame, uH​=−35q/36 and uCl​=q/36 for HCl; uD​=−35q/37 and uCl​=2q/37 for DCl. These ratios explain which partner moves and are separate from the change in frequency.
The common-k assumption belongs to the leading Born-Oppenheimer approximation: fixed nuclear positions and electric charges determine the electronic potential energy, while nuclear masses govern motion on that curve. Quantitative comparison requires actual atomic masses, departures from that approximation, and separation of anharmonicity and molecular rotation from the measured band. Even with common k, the quantum harmonic oscillator predicts a different zero-point energy for each isotope.[ref]

For a diatomic bond stretch, expand the body-axis dipole component as d(q)=de​+de′​q+⋯. A changing electric dipole moment, rather than a permanent value de​ alone, permits the harmonic fundamental. Keeping only the linear term and harmonic wavefunctions gives Δv=±1.[ref]
The derivation is sharper than a picture of a shaking molecule. Orthogonality removes the constant term for v′=v, and creation and annihilation operators give
⟨v′∣q∣v⟩=2μωℏ​​(v+1​δv′,v+1​+v​δv′,v−1​).

A nonzero vibrational matrix element is only one factor: rotational electric-dipole selection rules, initial populations, and spectral resolution also constrain visibility.
For an isolated diatomic molecule with identical atomic nuclei, such as molecular hydrogen in its symmetric electronic ground state, stretching preserves zero electric dipole moment. By symmetry, this homonuclear stretch is infrared inactive in the ideal dipole model, although it still vibrates. Other interactions or environments can permit detection.[ref]

Molecular vibration OurBigBook.com
The University of Florida's Rotation Vibration Spectrum of the HCl Molecule, University of Florida laboratory protocol, printed pp. 2–3 and 10–11, uses a scanning Michelson interferometer for Fourier transform spectroscopy. An air-filled silicon-window cell supplies the background. Supervised preparation adds concentrated hydrogen chloride liquid; the cleaned cell subsequently receives DCl liquid. Acquisition settings are identical.
The readout is transmission or absorbance against spectroscopic wavenumber, resolving molecular rotation alongside stretching. Background addresses instrument and cell contributions; cleaning addresses carryover. Excessive absorption impairs analysis. Assigning isotopes and rotational branches precedes fitting band parameters to test isotope scaling of diatomic vibration. These are prescribed measurements, not numerical observations supplied here.[ref]
For a transparent ideal model, add the linear rigid rotor to the harmonic vibrational energy levels and assume the same frequency-valued rotational constant B in both vibrational states:
Ev,J​=V0​+hνharm​(v+1/2)+hBJ(J+1).

For stipulated dimensionless values νharm​=100 and B=1, the first three R-branch positions are 102,104,106, and the first three P-branch positions are 98,96,94. There is no J=0→−1 transition. The numbers illustrate level subtraction; they are not HCl measurements. Real upper and lower rotational constants differ, and centrifugal distortion shifts lines further.

A vibrational overtone excites more than one vibrational quantum: v=0→2 is the first overtone, and 0→3 the second. Such transitions vanish in the combined harmonic-potential and linear-dipole approximation. Anharmonicity changes wavefunctions and level spacing; nonlinear terms in the electric dipole moment can also supply otherwise missing transition matrix elements.[ref]
For an original illustrative level model, set
Ev​−V0​=ℏω[(v+1/2)−ϵ(v+1/2)2],0<ϵ≪1.

Then E1​−E0​=ℏω(1−2ϵ) and E2​−E0​=2ℏω(1−3ϵ). With chosen ϵ=0.02, the fundamental gap is 0.96ℏω and the first-overtone gap 1.88ℏω, below twice the fundamental, 1.92ℏω. This low-level illustration does not determine transition intensity or justify extrapolation to arbitrarily large v. Molecular geometry

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Molecule OurBigBook.com
Why do methane, ammonia, and water have different shapes when each central chemical atom is surrounded by eight valence electrons? The answer separates the positions of atomic nuclei from the electron domains used in a VSEPR model.
Molecular geometry describes the three-dimensional arrangement of the atomic nuclei in a molecule, including bond lengths and bond angles. For a larger molecule, a shape name often describes just the neighbours of one central chemical atom. A Lewis structure records connections and electron bookkeeping; its flat layout does not fix molecular geometry.
In the VSEPR model, electron pair geometry includes both bonding electron domains and lone pairs, whereas molecular geometry counts only the chemical atoms. In methane, four bond pairs and no lone pairs give tetrahedral molecular geometry. In ammonia, three bond pairs and one lone pair give trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry. In water, two bond pairs and two lone pairs give bent molecular geometry. All three use the same ideal tetrahedral electron pair geometry; this does not make their actual bond angles equal. See Flowers, Theopold, Langley and Robinson, Chemistry 2e, §7.6: electron-pair and molecular geometries.
A static drawing also needs a physical interpretation. The atomic nuclei undergo oscillations; an arrangement at a minimum of potential energy and an experimentally averaged arrangement need not have identical bond lengths or bond angles. This distinction matters when comparing measurements with quantum mechanics calculations; see the IUPAC Gold Book: experimental bond-length conventions. Gas electron diffraction gives a concrete route from a laboratory signal to molecular geometry rather than inferring shape from a drawing alone.

In octahedral molecular geometry, six donor directions point toward the vertices of an octahedron. Three mutually cis donors can occupy one face; three coplanar donor directions can occupy a meridian.

Bond angle (θ)

Words: 176
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
A bond angle is the angle between two chemical bonds sharing a central chemical atom. In H–O–H, the middle symbol identifies the vertex: the angle is at oxygen. Let u and v be the nonzero displacement vectors from that atomic nucleus to the two neighbours. The actual three-dimensional bond angle satisfies
cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​,0≤θ≤π,
(36)
using the dot product and Euclidean norm. Rotating the whole molecule preserves this expression; projecting it onto a page generally does not.
There is another useful way to find a bond angle. If the two bond lengths are a,b and the distance between the outer atomic nuclei is d, the law of cosines gives
d2=a2+b2−2abcosθ.
(37)
For equal bond lengths a=b, this becomes d=2bsin(θ/2). Thus a measured outer-atom separation contains information about a bond angle even though those outer chemical atoms are not directly joined by a chemical bond.
For a stipulated rigid, equal-bond length model using water's 104.4776∘ equilibrium bond angle, d/b≈1.5811, whereas a straight H–O–H arrangement would give d/b=2. These are calculated geometric ratios, not new measured distances. Gas electron diffraction illustrates how pair-distance information can constrain molecular geometry. Substituting independently averaged distances into the rigid triangle formula does not automatically recover an equilibrium bond angle, because averaging and this nonlinear calculation need not commute.

Tetrahedral molecular geometry

Words: 186
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In tetrahedral molecular geometry, four neighbouring chemical atoms surround a central chemical atom in the directions of the vertices of a tetrahedron. In the regular idealization, the central atomic nucleus lies at the centre of a regular tetrahedron, and every pair of chemical bonds makes the same bond angle. Methane, CH4​, provides the standard example: its carbon has four bonding electron domains and no lone pair. See Chemistry 2e, §7.6: tetrahedral methane.
The exact ideal bond angle follows from four directions proportional to (1,1,1), (1,−1,−1), (−1,1,−1), and (−1,−1,1). Each has squared Euclidean norm 3, and each distinct pair has dot product −1. Hence
θ=arccos(−1/3)≈109.4712∘.
(38)
This is a statement about a regular tetrahedron, rather than a universal exact value for every molecule labelled tetrahedral. It also explains why a cross-shaped flat drawing with 90∘ gaps is misleading: four equal directions can spread out more evenly in three dimensions.
The same vectors sum to zero. Consequently, four equal bond-dipole contributions along those directions cancel. The symmetric methane molecule is nonpolar, but a tetrahedral shape alone does not imply a nonpolar molecule: replacing one neighbour can make the electronic distribution and bond contributions unequal. Chemical polarity depends on both molecular geometry and electron density. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, §2.2: molecular dipoles and methane.

Trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry

Words: 191
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry, three neighbouring chemical atoms form a triangular base and the central chemical atom lies outside its plane. The pyramid has four atomic nuclei; its central chemical atom is the apex, not the centre of the base. Ammonia, NH3​, has this arrangement. The [ref] lists an H–N–H bond angle of 106.67∘, commonly rounded to 106.7∘ or about 107∘.
The Lewis structure of ammonia allocates eight valence electrons as three bond pairs and one lone pair. Four electron domains therefore suggest tetrahedral electron pair geometry; removing the lone pair marker leaves three hydrogen chemical atoms below nitrogen. The VSEPR model treats the lone pair as more space-demanding and predicts compression relative to 109.4712∘, but it does not calculate the precise 106.67∘ value. See Chemistry 2e, §7.6: lone-pair effects.
Three equal bond-dipole contributions in this pyramid cancel sideways, but retain a component along its axis. By contrast, three equal contributions lying in one plane at 120∘ would cancel completely. This shows how a small change in molecular geometry can permit a permanent electric dipole moment. Ammonia is a polar molecule; NIST lists a measured magnitude of about 1.476 debye in the same [ref]. The vector argument predicts allowed direction and cancellation, not the full measured magnitude.

Bent molecular geometry

Words: 192
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
In bent molecular geometry, two neighbours and their central chemical atom form a noncollinear triangle, with an interior bond angle strictly between 0∘ and 180∘. Water, H2​O, is the standard example. The NIST CCCBDB experimental water entry, internal coordinates, citing Hoy and Bunker (1979) gives the equilibrium H–O–H bond angle as 104.4776∘ with quoted uncertainty 0.0019∘, usually rounded to 104.5∘.
The oxygen in water has two bonding electron domains and two lone pairs. Its ideal electron pair geometry is tetrahedral, while the three atomic nuclei give bent molecular geometry. Three points always lie in a plane; this does not make the four-domain scaffold planar. Nor does the word bent by itself determine an electron domain count: the same atomic shape can arise from other domain arrangements.
In an illustrative model with two equal bond-dipole contributions of magnitude p separated by bond angle θ, their sum of vectors points along the bisector and has magnitude 2pcos(θ/2). At 180∘ it vanishes; at 104.4776∘ it is approximately 1.2247p. This ratio is a geometric calculation, not a prediction of water's measured electric dipole moment. The entire electron density, including contributions represented by lone pairs, matters. Water is a polar molecule; chemical polarity helps explain its interactions with other polar molecules. See McMurry, Organic Chemistry, §2.2: water, lone-pair contributions, and polarity.

Gas electron diffraction

Words: 561
Molecular geometry OurBigBook.com
Gas electron diffraction infers molecular geometry from the diffraction of electrons by a gaseous sample. It makes a useful experimental test of shape: distances between both bonded and nonbonded atomic nuclei affect the signal, so a proposed straight arrangement and a bent arrangement can be distinguished through their pair separations.
A concrete modern apparatus is the Bielefeld instrument described by [ref]. A hot cathode supplies electrons; apertures and magnetic lenses shape the beam. A temperature-controlled nozzle injects sample vapour across it inside a vacuum chamber. Pumps and a cold trap reduce unwanted residual gas. A central beam stop catches the strong unscattered beam; off-axis scattered electrons expose imaging plates. A rotating sector can attenuate the intense small-angle region to accommodate detector range. The authors checked both the spatial scale of the plate scanner and its response to electron dose. These checks matter because an error in detector position or intensity calibration can masquerade as a structural difference.
What is measured is detector signal as a function of position, converted to scattering angle using the sample-to-detector distance. Randomly oriented molecules give radial information. After extracting the molecular intensity, compare it with predictions from a candidate arrangement and adjust the bond lengths and bond angles to improve the fit. The Wann Electron Diffraction Group's account of time-averaged GED, experiment and theory describes radial averaging and this refinement. The apparatus does not photograph one molecule with labelled atomic nuclei.
Why can distances survive random orientation? In a simplified rigid pair model with separation r, write s for the magnitude of the difference between incident and scattered wave vectors. Averaging the interference factor over uniformly distributed directions gives
21​∫−11​cos(srt)dt=srsin(sr)​,
(39)
with limiting value one at sr=0. This follows by integrating the cosine; t is the cosine of the angle between the pair and the scattering direction. The oscillations depend on r, although the orientation has disappeared. A real calculation weights many pairs by their scattering amplitudes and includes nuclear motion. The wave interference explanation and superposed pair-distance contributions are discussed in the same [ref].
Once a consistent structural model supplies two equal bond lengths b and an outer-atom separation d, the law of cosines converts these to a bond angle. For example, the illustrative d/b=1.5811 corresponds to approximately 104.5∘, while d/b=2 is straight. This geometric step explains what a shape measurement is trying to establish; it is not a new water measurement.
There are two essential limits. First, recovering labelled three-dimensional positions from a summed radial signal is an inverse problem: composition, candidate connectivity, and other structural information can be needed to distinguish competing fits. Karle's authored review Structure determination of gaseous and amorphous substances by diffraction methods (1977), abstract explains why too few independent observations make supplementary structural information indispensable. A good fit alone does not prove that the proposed arrangement is unique. Second, atomic nuclei are moving. Distances inferred by gas electron diffraction are motion-dependent averages; corrections are required before identifying them with a minimum-potential energy arrangement. For experimental distance conventions, see the IUPAC Gold Book: bond length. These limitations explain why model assumptions and the averaging convention must accompany a precise bond angle.

Nucleoside

Words: 104 Articles: 4
Molecule OurBigBook.com
A nucleoside combines a nucleobase with a sugar, without the phosphate groups of a nucleotide. Adenosine is the nucleoside built from adenine and ribose. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: nucleosides and nucleotides.

Thymidine

Nucleoside OurBigBook.com

Bromodeoxyuridine

Words: 18
Nucleoside OurBigBook.com
A brominated thymidine analogue incorporated during DNA synthesis. Substitution changes buoyant density, allowing copied strands to be distinguished from unsubstituted strands.

Inosine

Words: 19
Nucleoside OurBigBook.com
Inosine is the ribonucleoside of hypoxanthine. Hydrolytic deamination of adenosine replaces its exocyclic amino group with a carbonyl oxygen while retaining its sugar attachment.

Adenosine

Words: 36
Nucleoside OurBigBook.com
Adenosine consists of adenine joined to ribose. Adding one, two, or three phosphate groups at the ribose's 5′ position gives AMP, ADP, or ATP, respectively. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the components of nucleotides.

Nucleotide

Words: 1k Articles: 18
Molecule OurBigBook.com
A nucleotide contains a nucleobase, a sugar, and one or more phosphate groups. In DNA and RNA, linked nucleotides form a polymer whose nucleotide sequence carries information. The sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA. See NHGRI: nucleotide.

Nucleotide exchange

Words: 22
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
Replacement of a bound nucleotide by another. A changed exchange rate can alter a protein state without proving direct competition at the nucleotide-binding site.

Nucleotide sugar

Words: 227 Articles: 8
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
A nucleotide sugar carries an activated sugar linked to a nucleotide-containing group. It supports selective glycosyl transfer; donor identity alone does not specify the linkage or final glycan structure.

UDP-glucuronic acid

Words: 26
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
UDP-glucuronic acid is an activated donor containing a glucuronic acid residue linked to UDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

CMP-sialic acid

Words: 26
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
CMP-sialic acid is an activated donor containing a sialic acid residue linked to CMP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

ADP-glucose

Words: 24
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
ADP-glucose is an activated donor containing a glucose residue linked to ADP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

GDP-fucose

Words: 25
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
GDP-fucose is an activated donor containing a fucose residue linked to GDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

GDP-mannose

Words: 25
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
GDP-mannose is an activated donor containing a mannose residue linked to GDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine

Words: 25
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
UDP-N-acetylglucosamine is an activated donor containing a N-acetylglucosamine residue linked to UDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

UDP-galactose

Words: 25
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
UDP-galactose is an activated donor containing a galactose residue linked to UDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

UDP-glucose

Words: 24
Nucleotide sugar OurBigBook.com
UDP-glucose is an activated donor containing a glucose residue linked to UDP. Transfer requires an appropriate glycosyltransferase and acceptor; access to the correct compartment can be limiting.

(p)ppGpp

Words: 13
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
Collective notation for guanosine tetraphosphate and pentaphosphate alarmones involved in the bacterial stringent response.

Nucleoside triphosphate

Words: 13
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
A nucleoside carrying three phosphate groups. The relevant ribonucleoside triphosphates supply substrates for RNA polymerase.

Ribonucleotide

Words: 20
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
An RNA-type nucleotide containing ribose. Chemical modification can affect its contacts, pairing or recognition without changing its place in the transcript.

Guanosine diphosphate

Words: 25
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
guanosine diphosphate, abbreviated GDP, is the diphosphate form of a guanine nucleotide. Exchange between GDP and GTP, rather than receptor-catalyzed phosphorylation of GDP, controls the usual G protein switch.

Adenosine triphosphate (ATP)

Words: 521
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
ATP is a nucleotide consisting of adenosine, itself adenine joined to ribose, carrying three phosphate groups. From the ribose outward, these groups are labelled α, β, and γ. ATP connects energy-supplying processes to energy coupling for synthesis and active transport; the same carrier can be regenerated and reused. [ref].
The net hydrolysis commonly used in energy coupling is
ATP+H2​O⟶ADP+Pi​.
(40)
Here Pi​ denotes inorganic phosphate. At buffered pH 7, this biochemical shorthand groups the appropriate protonation states into pools and leaves proton exchange with the buffer solution implicit. An explicit, charge-balanced choice is ATP4−+H2​O⟶ADP3−+HPO4​2−+H+, without implying these are the only chemical species present. See the IUBMB recommendations for biochemical thermodynamics.
The quoted textbook biochemical standard state value is approximately
ΔG∘′=−30.5kJmol−1.
(41)
This convention uses fixed pH 7, temperature 298.15K (25∘C), reference pressure 100kPa (1bar), unit reference thermodynamic activities for dissolved reactants and reaction products, and water thermodynamic activity approximated by one. The prime indicates the fixed-pH biochemical convention. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 6.4: standard ATP hydrolysis value and Biology 2e, 6.2: biochemical standard conditions. This is a reference value, rather than a universal value inside a biological cell; precise tables must also specify chemical solution conditions and any magnesium ion binding convention. Different reference conventions and data treatments give different tabulated values, as discussed in Li et al., 2010: a database of thermodynamic quantities for biochemical reactions.
An exergonic reaction has a negative change in Gibbs free energy, so the overall ATP hydrolysis is favourable under those reference conditions. Breaking a chemical bond by itself costs energy; forming new chemical bonds can release energy. The net change compares all reactants with all reaction products, including their interactions with water and the entropy contribution. Calling the phosphate connection a "high-energy bond" describes a large favourable change in Gibbs free energy on hydrolysis, rather than energy released by bond breaking alone. See 7.5 Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds and Cooper, The Cell: ATP and metabolic energy.
Composition changes the driving force. At the same fixed pH, temperature, pressure, and binding convention, write the molar reaction change as
ΔG=ΔG∘′+RTlnQ,Q=aATP​aADP​aPi​​​.
(42)
Here R is the molar gas constant, T the absolute temperature, and a a dimensionless thermodynamic activity for a biochemical pool. Constant water thermodynamic activity is absorbed into the reference term; fixed pH accounts for buffered protons. The shorthand ΔG means transformed molar reaction Gibbs free energy change, Δr​G′, rather than a finite sample's total change. The natural logarithm acts on a dimensionless reaction quotient, never on concentrations with units. See the IUBMB biochemical thermodynamics recommendations and the general equilibrium constant relation.
For a stipulated ideal dilute chemical solution, let ai​=[i]/c∘, with c∘=1molL−1. Choose [ATP]=5mmolL−1, [ADP]=0.5mmolL−1, and [Pi​]=1mmolL−1, ignoring activity coefficient corrections and magnesium binding. These are illustrative inputs, not a claim about a particular biological cell. Then
Q=0.005(0.0005)(0.001)​=10−4,RT=(0.008314462618)(298.15)=2.47895703kJmol−1,
(43)
and
ΔG=−30.5+2.47895703ln(10−4)≈−53.332kJmol−1.
(44)
Increasing Q tenfold raises ΔG by RTln10≈5.708kJmol−1 at this temperature. Thus the ATP to ADP ratio and available inorganic phosphate matter, even with the same standard state value. These are local molar predictions at the stipulated composition, rather than a constant total yield as an isolated sample reacts.

Adenosine diphosphate (ADP)

Words: 136
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
ADP contains the same adenosine unit as ATP, with two phosphate groups instead of three. One ATP converted by the stated hydrolysis gives one ADP and one inorganic phosphate: 3=2+1 accounts for the phosphate groups while adenine and ribose are retained. ADP is therefore a reusable material carrier, rather than ATP with its entire structure discarded.
Regeneration reverses the net chemical reaction:
ADP+Pi​⟶ATP+H2​O.
(45)
At the same stipulated reference conditions its ΔG∘′ is +30.5kJmol−1, the negative of the hydrolysis value. It is an endergonic reaction and requires energy input through energy coupling; a catalyst alone cannot supply that input. Recycling the material carrier does not recycle the expended driving energy. Cellular respiration and light-dependent reactions supply routes for regeneration. See Cooper, The Cell: ATP generation and energy coupling.
ADP is a nucleotide with two phosphate groups. Formation of ATP from ADP and phosphate couples to energy supply in light-dependent reactions; the Calvin cycle returns ADP after using ATP. [ref].

Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)

Words: 30
Nucleotide OurBigBook.com
AMP is adenosine carrying one phosphate group at the ribose's 5′ position. The count distinguishes AMP from ADP with two and ATP with three; adenosine itself has none. See Cooper, The Cell: ATP, ADP, and AMP.
